title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
hook: who is the path of action actually for? the Uddhava Gita answers: people who still want things

segments.voice: Yesterday's karma lesson came from the ground: the earth gets pushed around all day and doesn't swerve. When something knocked into your day, did you keep to your path? Day one thousand two hundred four.
screen: `THE EARTH DOESN'T SWERVE.` · `WHO IS ACTION FOR?`

segments.voice: Who is the path of action actually for? It's a fair question, and deep in the dialogue Uddhava asks something close to it. The Vedas, he says in effect, tell people what to do and what not to do. They praise good works, and they also speak of a state beyond works altogether. So which is it? Do something, or stop doing? It sounds like a question that needs a side. Krishna doesn't pick one. He looks at the people asking. His answer sorts paths by who's walking them, and the path of action, karma, lands somewhere surprising.
screen: `DO SOMETHING, OR STOP DOING?` → `KRISHNA DOESN'T PICK A SIDE.` → `HE LOOKS AT THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Krishna says he has given three yogas, three paths, so that people can reach the good: the path of knowing, jnana; the path of action, karma; and the path of devotion, bhakti. Then comes the sorting. Jnana, he says, suits those who have grown weary of action and turned away from it. Karma suits those who haven't, whose hearts still hold desires, who still want things from the world. And bhakti suits someone who, by some good fortune, has come to love hearing about him, neither fed up with the world nor tied too tightly to it. Sit with that middle line. The path of action isn't reserved for finished saints. It's for people who still want things: people with ambitions, a to-do list, a pull toward the world. The Uddhava Gita doesn't scold that wanting. It gives it a road. And how long does a person stay on that road? The very next verse answers: keep doing the work until you grow weary of it, or until faith in hearing his stories wakes up. Two ways off the road, and no deadline. For someone in the middle of a busy life, this is a quietly kind teaching. It doesn't say: drop everything first, and then you can begin. It says: begin where your wanting already is. Work is the doorway for the one who still wants to work.
screen: `THREE PATHS: KNOWING, ACTION, LOVE.` · `ACTION IS FOR THOSE WHO STILL WANT.` · `STAY UNTIL WEARY, OR UNTIL FAITH WAKES.` · `BEGIN WHERE YOUR WANTING IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your wanting. Settle into the breath. Without judging it, let one thing you want rise up: a result at work, a change at home, something you're building. Don't push it away, and don't chase it. Just see it clearly, the way you'd look at a road from the top of a hill. Then ask: what's one honest piece of work this wanting is asking of me today? If you pray, you can offer that wanting, just as it is, to the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Karma. In the Uddhava Gita, the path of action: for people whose hearts still want things, walked until they grow weary or faith wakes up. Today's word.
Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. Today, pick one thing you want and do one honest piece of work toward it, without apologizing for wanting it. Day one thousand two hundred four.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers speak of three paths, jnana, karma and bhakti, and some say a student's temperament and stage of life help decide which path to emphasize, drawing on teachings like this one in the Bhagavata's eleventh book.

knowing for the weary, action for those still wanting, devotion for those who love hearing of him.

fork.setup: you're busy, ambitious and not tired of the world at all. which of the three paths does the Uddhava Gita say suits you?
options: none yet; come back when you're weary.
fork.reveal: karma: Krishna gives the path of action to people whose hearts still want things, and tells them to stay on it until weariness or faith arrives.

original.note: Sanskrit: the path, or discipline, of action; one of the three yogas Krishna names to Uddhava.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga is for people who have already let go of wanting.
what it means: in the Uddhava Gita, it's the road for those who still want things, walked until weariness or faith arrives.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 11.20.6–9, where the three yogas are matched to the weary, to those with desires still in the heart, and to those who love his stories.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.20.1–5 (Uddhava asks how the Veda's commands to act fit with its praise of what lies beyond action)
Bhagavata Purana 11.20.6–8 (three yogas: jnana for the weary of action, karma for those with desires, bhakti for those who by fortune love hearing of him)
Bhagavata Purana 11.20.9 (perform action until weariness arises or faith in hearing his stories awakens)

notes: Uddhava's question at 11.20.1–5 is paraphrased loosely (the Veda's injunctions and prohibitions vs. what lies beyond them); confirm the framing.
